target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would guarantee that many people can vote by removing work-schedule barriers
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably solve the work-schedule problem because private employers are not required to give paid time off or let workers leave shifts to vote. Many service and retail workers—especially low-income workers—would still have to work or lose wages, so the policy could leave the people it is meant to help still constrained by work and income penalties.

target: AG2’s assumption that a federal holiday would not meaningfully remove the scheduling barrier because employers control whether people get time off
objection: A holiday changes the default day-of schedule: schools typically close and many workplaces move to holiday schedules, so voters are no longer trying to fit voting into a normal weekday. That means the policy does address the scheduling barrier directly, rather than depending on special employer permission.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday would make the day off by default for most voters
objection: The assumption that a federal holiday turns Election Day into a true off-day is not guaranteed. Private employers can still keep operating and require employees to work, and school schedules are locally controlled, so the holiday status does not reliably eliminate the work/school barrier for many voters, especially low-income shift workers.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would only have limited impact because employer discretion still exists
objection: The objection overstates the importance of employer discretion. A national holiday changes the default schedule for the day, so many people are simply not working or in school, which removes the timing constraint for far more voters than a normal weekday does, even if some private businesses still operate.

target: AG1’s premise that a federal holiday means schools close and many workplaces stop or reduce hours by default
objection: That premise is unreliable because federal holiday status does not compel private employers to close, reduce shifts, or provide paid leave, and schools are locally scheduled. Many retail, service, and hourly workers would still be working, so the holiday would not uniformly remove the timing barrier.

target: AG2’s argument that a holiday would still disadvantage low-income workers because many could not take unpaid time off
objection: The holiday targets the underlying timing problem itself: when Election Day is treated as an off-day, many schools and workplaces shift schedules, so people do not need to miss a normal weekday shift or absorb lost wages in the same way. That especially helps low-income workers whose main barrier is rigid daytime scheduling.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday changes the default schedule for schools and many workplaces
objection: The schedule-shift premise is shaky because federal holiday status does not force private employers to close or alter staffing, and school closures are not guaranteed nationwide. Since many workers remain on regular shifts, the holiday does not reliably turn Election Day into a day when daytime voting is broadly available.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status does not reliably change schedules enough to matter
objection: A federal holiday does change the default schedule enough to matter: schools follow holiday schedules and many workplaces reduce hours or close, so a large share of voters can vote during the day without special permission. Even where some retail or service workers still work, the holiday increases practical accommodation and reduces the need to miss paid time.

target: AG1’s premise that federal holiday status guarantees schools close and many workplaces operate on holiday hours
objection: Federal holiday status mostly creates an expectation for government entities; it does not compel private employers to close, reduce shifts, or give paid time off. Many lower-income workers in retail and service jobs remain on similar schedules, so the policy does not reliably eliminate the work/school barrier.

target: AG2’s claim that a national holiday is a weak or inefficient turnout strategy compared with other reforms
objection: A national holiday directly reduces the timing barrier by moving Election Day off a normal weekday, and it also has broad support and international precedent. It can complement other reforms rather than compete with them, so it is not merely a symbolic or inferior approach.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday reliably removes the work-and-school timing barrier
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably change private-sector work schedules or guarantee paid leave, so many retail and service workers still face shift conflicts or income loss to vote. The more dependable fixes are laws that directly require time off to vote or other access reforms, rather than assuming holiday status will do the job.

target: AG2’s argument that the holiday is unreliable because some workers may still be scheduled
objection: The proposal does not depend on every private employer shutting down; it is enough that a holiday shifts the default conditions for schools and many workplaces so voting becomes feasible for far more people than on a regular weekday. It can also be paired with other reforms, so the fact that some workers still have schedules does not negate its direct effect.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday reliably eliminates the timing problem for the voters most affected by it
objection: The policy cannot guarantee that because many essential or consumer-facing jobs continue operating on holidays, and low-income workers often still have to work or use limited leave. Since private employers are not compelled to close or change staffing, the timing barrier is not consistently removed for the people who face it most.

target: AG2’s view that turning Election Day into a holiday only indirectly affects turnout and is mostly symbolic
objection: The holiday directly improves turnout by removing a concrete time-based barrier and by changing the social meaning of voting from a chore to a civic event. That behavioral change itself can increase participation, so the effect is not merely indirect or symbolic.

target: AG1’s assumption that changing Election Day into a civic celebration is a dependable way to raise turnout on its own
objection: Even if voting feels more celebratory, turnout still depends on practical access conditions such as work schedules, pay, leave, registration, and local voting access. A holiday cannot guarantee those conditions, so the psychological boost is not a reliable substitute for reforms that directly remove barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday only indirectly touches turnout barriers
objection: The holiday directly removes a real, time-based barrier by shifting Election Day off a normal work/school day, so people do not need exceptional leave to vote. It also can coexist with other reforms, meaning it is a direct access reform rather than only an indirect symbolic gesture.

target: AG1’s assumption that a federal holiday reliably changes work and school schedules enough to remove the timing barrier
objection: A federal holiday does not compel private employers to give paid time off or excuse workers from shifts, so many workers—especially in retail and service jobs—may still face the same practical barriers. Since the everyday schedules that matter to many voters are not consistently altered, the holiday does not reliably eliminate the constraint.

target: AG2’s suggestion that state-by-state access reforms are preferable because a holiday is not reliable enough
objection: A national holiday provides a uniform off-day standard across the country, whereas state-by-state reforms leave people dependent on different local rules, employer practices, and administrative arrangements. That makes the holiday a more direct and consistent way to address the scheduling barrier nationwide.
